Abstract 19

The global shift toward net-zero emissions necessitates resource recovery from wet 20

waste. In this study, we demonstrate the first feasibility of combining pilot-scale 21

microbial electrolytic cells (MECs) with hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) for 22

simultaneous post-hydrothermal liquefaction wastewater (PHW) treatment and 23

efficient hydrogen (H₂) production to meet biocrude upgrading requirements. Long- 24

term single reactor operation revealed that fixed anode potential enabled rapid startup, 25

and low catholyte pH and high salinity were effective in suppression of cathodic 26

methanogenesis and acetogenesis – resulting in high current density of 16.6 A m-2 and 27

9.3 A m-2 when feeding synthetic wastewater and PHW respectively. Additionally, the 28

anode biofilm exhibited spatial variations in response to local environmental conditions. 29

Onsite parallel or serial operations of multiple MECs showed good performance using 30

actual PHW with a record-high H2 production rate of 0.5 L LR day-1 for MEC over 10 31

liters scale, and the optimal chemical oxygen demand (COD)-to-H2 yield reached 0.127 32

kg-H2 per kg-COD, supporting a self-sufficient, closed-loop upgrade to jet fuel. 33

1. Introduction 37

As we strive to keep the fossil carbon underground, sustainable biomass emerges as a 38

crucial carbon source to enable carbon circulation and the transition to clean energy, 39

fuels, and chemicals (Jack et al., 2019; Lu and Ren, 2016). The current management 40

practices for wet waste, such as food waste, animal manure, and wastewater sludge, 41

consume significant energy but fail to recover high value products from the embedded 42

energy and carbon (Milbrandt et al., 2018). In this context, hydrothermal liquefaction 43

(HTL) emerged as a promising technology for wet waste treatment and valorization. 44

HTL transforms wet waste into biocrude oil under high pressure and moderate 45

temperature (Alper Basar et al., 2021), and after hydrotreating, the biocrude can be 46

upgraded to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). SAF is among the most desired products 47

from organic waste, as it has high value and significant market potential, addressing 48

one of the most challenging tasks of aviation sector decarbonization. However, HTL 49

currently faces several major technical challenges. The U.S. Department of Energy 50

identified the management of post-HTL wastewater (PHW) as a key barrier. This 51

wastewater is highly concentrated and contains recalcitrant nitrogen species, which 52

traditional wastewater treatment facilities struggle to treat (Jiang et al., 2023b; Wang et 53

al., 2024; Watson et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020). In addition, a substantial amount of 54

H2 is required to reduce heteroatoms (such as sulfur, nitrogen, and oxygen) in the 55

biocrude oil before it can be refined into SAF (Snowden-Swan et al., 2022). Currently, 56


<!-- Page 4 -->


most H2 supply comes from natural gas, which significantly undermines the 57

sustainability of the overall process (Global Hydrogen Review 2022, 2022). 58

59

Different treatment and valorization techniques have been explored for managing PHW, 60

including biological, hydrothermal, and integrated pathways (Watson et al., 2020). For 61

example, PHW can be used for biomass cultivation to grow algae or crops, with the 62

captured carbon from biomass further utilized as food and biofuel (Zhou et al., 2013). 63

However, this method requires extensive land area, and commonly requires heavy 64

dilution to avoid growth inhibitions (Watson et al., 2020). Alternatively, hydrothermal 65

gasification can be applied to PHW to produce energy-rich gas. Although this process 66

is fast and efficient, it demands a stringent reactor design and high energy input (Watson 67

et al., 2017). Plus, these processes don’t resolve the issue of H2 demand. In this context, 68

integrating microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) with HTL stands out as an especially 69

attractive solution. By leveraging microbial metabolism and electrochemical H2 70

production, MECs can simultaneously treat the recalcitrant wastewater while producing 71

clean H2 for onsite biocrude upgrading, thereby creating a closed-loop process (Fig. 1A) 72

(Jiang et al., 2022; Wang and Ren, 2013). Our previous works demonstrated that lab- 73

scale MECs can produce up to 1.62 L L-1 d-1 H2 using PHW as feedstock, achieving a 74

COD removal rate up to 98% for the recalcitrant stream (Jiang et al., 2023b; Shen et al., 75

2018). However, the real-world potential has not been verified as scaling-up often 76

comes up with unique challenges such as limited current density, and compromised 77


<!-- Page 5 -->


long-term stability (Jiang et al., 2023a). More importantly, the previous scale-up efforts 78

of MEC often produce H2 as a standalone product without a contextual need. Although 79

H2 consumption is expected to increase in the coming decades, finding an onsite use 80

case that balances the supply and demand still holds great advantage as transportation 81

of H2 remains an expensive and emission-intensive process (Global Hydrogen Review 82

2022, 2022; Winter et al., 2022). Therefore, demonstrating a proof-of-concept closed- 83

loop integration with a pilot HTL system would set a precedent for more fit-for-purpose 84

bioelectrochemical H₂ production. 85

86

In this study, we present the first pilot integration of MECs with HTL system. We 87

designed a symmetric rectangular reactor module featuring two anode chambers and 88

one cathode chamber. Each reactor module has a total capacity over 80 liters and a 89

working volume of 55 liters. To assess the suitability of PHW as an MEC substrate and 90

the challenges of scaling up the process, we conducted long-term and onsite operations 91

using actual PHW from HTL reactors processing food waste. Satisfying organic 92

removal and H2 production were obtained, and the close-loop biocrude upgrading 93

without external H2 supply was achieved with optimal COD-to-H2 yield. 94

2. Materials and methods 95

2.1. Pilot MEC assembly 96

In total, four reactor modules were manufactured, one for in-lab long-term 97

operation, and three for onsite operation. Each reactor module (110 cm×13 cm×60 cm) 98

came in rectangular shape with reactor frames manufactured from 99


<!-- Page 6 -->


acrylic.(“Performance of a pilot-scale continuous flow microbial electrolysis cell fed 100

winery wastewater | Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology,” n.d.) Each module was 101

divided into three chambers with two anode chambers (100 cm×4 cm×50 cm each) on 102

the side and one cathode chamber (100 cm×3 cm×50 cm) in the middle. Two back 103

plates (each 1 cm wide) enclosed the chambers by sandwiching the two anode chamber 104

frames and one cathode chamber frame in between. Nineteen carbon brush anodes (60 105

cm long with 10 cm bare end and a carbon brush diameter of 4 cm) were evenly inserted 106

into each anode chamber and were connected by wire connector blocks (Jandeccn) 107

through 14-gauge wires. Before insertion, the carbon anode brushes were heat-treated 108

at 450 ℃ for 30 min.(Feng et al., 2010) Stainless steel wire cloth (316 SS, 60×60 mesh 109

size, 0.009" opening size, McMaster-Carr) were used as cathode. The wire cloth was 110

cut into 78 cm×26 cm size (2,000 cm2 cross section area) and fixed with titanium wire 111

(0.031" Diameter, 1/4 lb. Coil, McMaster-Carr) for connection with potentiostat and 112

power supply. The working volume of each anode and cathode chamber is 20 L and 15 113

L, respectively. The anode chamber and cathode chamber were separated by cation 114

exchange membrane (CXM-200, Membrane International Inc.). Before application, the 115

membrane is first preconditioned in 5% NaCl solution for 12 hours for hydration and 116

expansion. Due to the large cross section area (5,000 cm2) of the module, three 117

supporting structures were evenly distributed in each anode chamber to prevent 118

membrane deformation while minimizing water blockage (Fig. S1). 119

2.3. MEC operation 136

For inoculation, anodic effluent containing electroactive bacteria (EABs) from in- 137

lab MECs were mixed with MEC anolyte (1:1 v/v) containing sodium acetate to serve 138

as the inoculum.(Bian et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023b) The MEC anolyte contains 100 139

mM phosphate buffer solution (PBS, 9.16 g L−1 Na2HPO4 and 4.90 g L−1 NaH2PO4), 140

4.92 g L-1 sodium acetate, mineral solution (12.5 mL L-1) and vitamin solutions (5 mL 141

L-1) (Jiang et al., 2022). Two different inoculation strategies were explored in this study: 142

fixed-voltage and fixed-potential. In fixed-voltage inoculation, 1.2 V was applied 143

across each module by DC power supply (Keithley 2260B-720W) (Lu et al., 2015). In 144

fixed-potential inoculation, the anodes were poised at a constant potential at -0.35 V vs. 145

Ag/AgCl reference electrode using potentiostat (Biologic, France) (Zhu et al., 2022). 146

In both strategies, inoculum was only added at the beginning of the inoculation. 147

148

After successful inoculation, each module was connected to one power supply. The 149

current was recorded by measuring the voltage drop across a 0.1 Ω resistor electrically 150

connected in-series with the module. In lab-scale studies, the voltage across the reactor 151

is often considered equal to the voltage set at the power supply as the voltage loss across 152

the wire and the resistor is negligible. However, this voltage loss due to resistance can 153

be significant at pilot scale as the current is much higher. As a reference, a 1-amp 154

current would lead to 100 mV voltage loss across the 0.1 Ω resistor, a significant loss 155

considering MEC uses relatively small voltages (oftentimes 300 – 1,000 mV). 156

Therefore, the actual voltage across the MEC module is also recorded by potentiostat 157


<!-- Page 9 -->


to account for the loss in the circuit. The cathode gas was collected using a gas bag 158

(Calibrated Instrument) attached to the cathodic chamber. The gas components were 159

analyzed with a gas chromatography with TCD detector (SRI310, SRI Instrument) with 160

UHP N2 as carrier gas (Jack et al., 2022). 161

For the long-term operation, one MEC module (R-single) was operated for three months. 163

R-single was operated in a continuous, 100% recirculation manner with an anolyte flow 164

rate of 50 L day-1 and a catholyte flow rate of 20 L day-1. A continuous system would 165

improve mass transfer, but would also bring additional challenges such as increased H2 166

loss and membrane deformation. However, we alleviated membrane deformation 167

through supporting structure (Section 2.1) and did not observe significant H2 loss 168

throughout the experiments. The catholyte was 100 mM PBS, and the anolyte was 169

started with synthetic wastewater during startup then switched to PHW-GFW diluted 170

with 100 mM PBS to maintain influent COD at around 4,000 mg L-1. The anolyte and 171

catholyte were operated with their own liquid loop with automatic pH adjusting with a 172

dosing station, and each loop contains a recirculation bottle as reservoir. The anolyte 173

and catholyte pH were initially all set at 7.0, but the catholyte pH was further dosed 174

down to 4.0 to inhibit acetogens during the operation (see Section 3.1.3 for details). 175

The pH adjustment was done by digital pH controllers (Bluelab, USA) connected to 176

sulfuric acid (50% v/v, for cathode pH control) or sodium hydroxide solution (50% w/v, 177

for anode pH control). The COD was continuously monitored and when the COD value 178


<!-- Page 10 -->


fell under 500 mg L-1, the recirculation bottle was refilled with new substrates. All 179

aqueous solutions were prepared with DI water. 180

181

After gaining insights and experience from R-single operation, onsite pilot operation 182

was carried out. Three identical MEC modules (R1, R2 and R3) were fabricated and 183

operated inside the same building that houses the pilot HTL reactor. Similar operation 184

strategy was implemented, with the EAB cultures inoculated from the R-single reactor 185

and initially enriched with synthetic wastewater. After reactors were stabilized 186

(reaching a platform in current density), they were fed with diluted PHW-SDW that has 187

a COD around 5,000 mg L-1. The cathode liquid loop was operated continuously with 188

100% recirculation and kept at pH = 4 using a pH dosing station. The anode liquid loop 189

loop were investigated. During in-parallel operation, each module was applied a voltage 193

of 0.7 V. During in-series operation, R1, R2 and R3 were supplied with 0.9 V, 0.7 V 194

and 0.5 V voltage, respectively. The rationale behind this strategy is detailed in Section 195

3.3.1. The overall hydraulic retention time (HRT) was kept at 72 hr, meaning that the 196

HRT for each module was 72 hr during in-parallel operation and 24 hr during in-series 197

operation. Schematics drawing of the operational modes can be found in Section 3.3. 198

3. Results and discussion 251

3.1. Long-term operation of a single pilot MEC 252

3.1.1. Fixed-potential inoculation allows fast start-up 253

Previous studies have suggested that anode potential directly affects biofilm 254

development. While a low anode potential thermodynamically hinders the electron 255

transfer process, a high anode potential may promote the growth of non-electroactive 256

competitors to EABs (Torres et al., 2009). In the start-up of R-single, we chose an anode 257

potential of -0.35 V vs. Ag/AgCl, as it has shown to stimulate a biofilm primarily 258

composed of electroactive Geobacter spp. However, such setting at the pilot scale 259

overloads the potentiostat, which has a current limit of 800 mA. The overload was due 260

to the charging of the electric double layer, which occurs when the electrode potential 261

changes. Therefore, we deployed a stepwise method to gradually decrease the anode 262

potential to the desired value (Fig. 2). With such a strategy, we observed a swift startup 263

with current density quickly went up to a maximum over 3 A m-2 within a week. 264

Following that, the current gradually decreased despite us regularly monitoring COD 265

concentration and replenishing substrate when COD went low. It was discovered that 266

such current decrease was due to the pH change during operation. In 22 days, the 267

cathodic pH rose to above 12, while the anodic pH dropped to 5. To address this, we 268


<!-- Page 15 -->


added the pH dosing to the recirculation loop and immediately observed an increase in 269

current, which exceeded 800 mA within 2 days. Consequently, we then switched to 270

power supply for fixed-voltage operation (Fig. 2) . 271

3.1.2. Long term performance of the R-single 281

The R-single showed good performance overall under different operational conditions. 282

The highest current density achieved was 16.6 A m-2 and 9.3 A m-2, respectively, when 283

the reactor was fed with synthetic wastewater and actual PHW-GFW, respectively (Fig. 284

3A). This current density is only slightly lower than the maximum achieved in the 285

previous lab-scale study fed with PHW (~ 20 A m-2) and exceeded that of most lab- 286

scale MECs – which typically have a current density < 10 A m-2 (Jiang et al., 2023b; 287

Tang et al., 2022). When comparing with previous pilot MECs, the current density 288

successful inhibition of methanogens and acetogens in the cathode, which will be 299

discussed in Section 3.1.3. The decrease in current density when using PHW-GFW is 300

due to the complexity of the substrate. PHW-GFW was derived from a grocery store 301

food waste mixture, which contains a variety of organic compounds such as saccharides, 302

protein, and fatty acids. The resulting PHW therefore contained organics that may not 303

be readily available to EABs, such as glycerol which is present in high concentration in 304

PHW-GFW (Table 1). Rather, they were first undergoing fermentation, with the 305

resulting fermentation products subsequently utilized by EABs. Our previous study 306

revealed the exact microbial PHW degradation process (Jiang et al., 2023b). 307

Additionally, the presence of sugars and proteins in the food waste mixture leads to the 308

formation nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds through Maillard reaction, 309

which is potentially toxic to EABs. The R-single reactor reliably achieved COD 310

removal above 60% within a week under synthetic wastewater (Fig. 3C). The fastest 311

kinetics was observed from day 50 to 53 where an 85% COD removal was achieved 312

within 3 days. After switching to PHW-GFW, the COD removal kinetics slowed down, 313

indicated by the gentler slope of anode COD profile (Fig. 3C). However, with an ample 314

HRT, R-single was still able to achieve > 70% COD removal under an applied voltage 315

of 0.55 V, and > 85% COD removal under 0.73 and 0.99 V. We recorded the actual 316

applied voltage on the reactor instead of directly reading the set voltage of the power 317

supply as the ohmic loss could be significant in larger scale systems due to large current. 318

One key advantage of MEC compared to abiotic electrolysis for H2 production is the 320

much lower energy consumption by leveraging the chemical energy embedded in 321

wastewater. This advantage holds true in pilot operation as well. The highest energy 322

consumption observed by R-single was 26 kWh kg-H2-1 under an actual applied voltage 323

of 0.99 V (Fig. 3D), which is only about half of the energy needed by a state-of- 324

technology water electrolyzer (50 kWh kg-H2-1) (Technical Targets for Proton 325

Exchange Membrane Electrolysis, n.d.). As the energy consumption is determined by 326

the input voltage and 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 (see Section 2.4 for derivation) and 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 has been relatively 327

stable, the energy consumption scales directly with the input voltage, reducing to 16 328

kWh kg-H2-1 at 0.55 V (Fig. 3D). Such low energy consumption is significant, as the 329

cost of water electrolysis is primarily driven by electricity cost. 330

In the HTL process, a considerable amount of nitrogen in the feedstock ends up in the 332

PHW, resulting in high nitrogen concentrations, typically in the thousands of ppm. 333

Moreover, most of the nitrogen in PHW-GFW is organic nitrogen (ORG-N), which 334

adding additional difficulty in treatment and making most existing treatment processes 335

ineffective (Table 1). We measured the nitrogen removal profile under different 336

voltages and found that the removal efficiency is positively correlated with the applied 337

voltage (Fig. 3E-F). This is mainly due to the improved removal of NH3-N at higher 338

H2 was converted into CH4 at latter stage (Cusick et al., 2011; He et al., 2022). Even 367

still occur due to the diffused H2 into the cathode chamber (Guerrero-Sodric et al., 369

2023). In our system, however, no methanogenesis was observed throughout the 370

operation, evidenced by zero CH4 peak identified in GC analysis and almost 100% 371

purity H2 (Fig. 3B). We believe the strong inhibition of methanogens without adding 372

inhibitors was achieved by the low pH in the cathode chamber. The optimal pH for 373

methanogens is near neutral (6.8-7.5), whereas slightly acidic pH has been shown to 374

inhibit methanogens. In our experiments, cathodic pH was gradually adjusted to 5 after 375

starting pH control (Fig. S2), which would be sufficiently acidic to inhibit growth of 376

methanogens. In addition, the lower pH of the catholyte also facilitates H2 production 377

with the abundance of protons availability. Interestingly, 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 still exhibits a decrease 378

down to 53% during Day 30 to Day 50, accompanied by a gradual COD increase in 379

catholyte up to 2,090 mg L-1 (Fig. 3C). Theoretically, catholyte COD should be close 380

to 0 as neither buffer (PBS) nor the dosing solution (sulfuric acid solution) would 381

contribute to COD. The CEM should also be able to block most, if not all, COD- 382

contributing ions. Therefore, two possible reasons exist for COD increase in this period: 383

1. Compromised CEM allowed crossover of co-ions (anions); 2. Acetogens growth in 384

the cathode chamber. Upon further investigation, we believe the growth of the 385

acetogens was the major factor that contributed to cathodic COD increase. This is 386


<!-- Page 21 -->


supported by several evidence. Firstly, the HPLC analysis of the catholyte revealed a 387

major peak of acetate, but no significant peak of other organics was observed. Should 388

the CEM be compromised, the catholyte COD compositions should be much more 389

complex. Secondly, the decreased 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 flagged that H2 was being utilized. Since 390

methanogenic behavior was not observed, the acetogens were the most likely 391

candidates for H2 utilization. Lastly, the cathode recirculation bottle also became turbid 392

during the same period (Fig. S3A-B), suggesting microbial growth. Upon examination 393

under optical microscope, we did observe short rod-shaped cells, of which many occurs 394

in pairs (Fig. S3C) – a morphology known to be possessed by Acetobacterium spp. The 395

16S rRNA gene sequencing further proved growth of acetogens in the cathodic chamber, 396

which will be discussed in Section 3.2. 397

398

Unlike methanogens, which have been a thorny issue in MEC operation, the occurrence 399

of acetogens was reported much less frequently in MEC literature (Parameswaran et al., 400

2012, 2011; Ruiz et al., 2013). Our experimental condition might have set up a niche 401

that suits acetogens but prevents methanogenic growth due to its acidic catholyte. 402

Though consuming H2 by acetogens converted CO2 to acetate make the reactor 403

practically performs microbial electrosynthesis (MES) (Bian et al., 2024), it is not the 404

goal of this study on maximizing H2 production. Accordingly, starting Day 45, we 405

further dosed down the cathodic pH to 4 in an attempt to inhibit acetogens while 406

boosting H2 production. The pH control was successful as cathodic COD started to 407

continuously decrease owing to consumption by acetate-oxidizing bacteria, and 408

consequentially the improvement of 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐, which went back to > 80% after dosing down 409

the cathodic pH. The development of acetogens did not recur during the remaining 410

experimental period. 411

Our approach here showcased a successful inhibition of methanogens and acetogens in 413

long-term operation without dosing specific inhibitor, such as the commonly used 414

methanogen inhibitor 2-bromoethanesulfonate (BES). Besides pH effect, we also 415

believe that the high salinity partially contributed to the inhibition of these H2- 416

consuming microbes in the cathode. Because of the continuous pH dosing and 417

recirculation, the salinity of the catholyte gradually increased in the initial period, 418

mS cm-1), the microbes might not be well suited for saline environment. Most, if not 421

all, MECs fed with saline electrolyte were inoculated from saline environments, such 422

as salt marsh. 423

3.2. Spatial heterogeneity of biofilm ecology in the pilot reactor 424

We collected biofilm samples from different sections of the anodes, as well as 425

suspended samples from cathode chamber during the cathode COD anomaly period. 426

The exact location of sampling is shown in Figure 4A. All anodic samples yielded 427

sufficient reads except for sample A32. In a pilot module, the spatial heterogeneity can 428

be observed both horizontally and vertically. In the anode chamber, the upper sections 429

of each anode are exposed to higher dissolved O2 and are closer to the power source. 430

Consequently, the anode potential exhibits a slight decrease along the depth (Fig. S5), 431

Horizontally, the anodes closer to the inlet are exposed to higher COD availability than 432

those further down the length. Such spatial variability in operation acts as selection 433

pressure toward the microbiome composition. Accordingly, the sequencing results 434

showed a much higher vertical heterogeneity compared to horizontally (Fig. 4B). Most 435

notably, from depth 2 (the middle point along the depth) further down, biofilm primarily 436

composed of Geobacter spp. was formed and in some sampling points, such genus 437

could account for almost 100% abundance (samples A22-A24, A33, A34 and B12). 438

Even in the least abundant sample B34, Geobacter spp. still accounted for 45% of the 439

reads. In contrast, samples taken from the top generally showed much higher microbial 440

diversity. Aerobes and facultative anaerobes such as Rhodococcus spp. (74% 441

abundance in A12), Azospirillum spp. (48% abundance in A13) and Dysgonomonas spp. 442

(42% abundance in A11) were found in significant abundance. When aggregated to the 443

depth, we could see a clear pattern of vertical heterogeneity, where the top samples 444

showed a distinct profile from samples taken from the middle and the bottom (Fig. 4C). 445

The dominance of Geobacter spp. from the middle down to the bottom was a result 446

of two selection pressures (Fig. 4D). The decreased DO along the depth would select 447

for anaerobes and prohibit the growth of aerobes. Moreover, as the anode potential went 448

more negative along the depth, it posed a strong selection pressure for Geobacter spp. 449

and discourage the growth of non-electroactive microbes and electroactive microbes 450

that can’t survive on low electron acceptor (anode) potentials. It should also be noted 451

that the sole methanogens identified - Methanobrevibacter spp. – were only found in 452

where no methanogenic activity was found throughout the operation (Section 3.1.3). 454

The two cathode suspended samples showed the same profile – 100% 457

3.3.1. Onsite reactor performance 495

The pilot modules were directly inoculated using constant-potential control, 496

with anode potential set at -0.35 V vs Ag/AgCl reference electrode. All three reactors 497

showed rapid start-up with current density reached >1 A m-2 within three days of 498

inoculation (Fig. 6A). We believe the fast start-up was owing to the beneficial 499

temperature (30 ℃), the right inoculum from preacclimated reactors, and the proper 500

applied anode potential. The pilot modules were operated with synthetic wastewater 501

using sodium acetate until day 12, to allow for ample acclimation of the microbial 502

community. From then on, PHW-SDW diluted to a COD of 5,000 mg L-1 was used as 503

anolyte. During in-parallel operation, all three modules were exposed to the same COD 504

concentration at the inlet. As expected, R2 and R3 exhibited similar current density 505

profiles with a maximum current density of 8.7 A m-2 (Fig. 6B). R1, however, started 506

with similar current density then went through a drastic increase followed by a drop, 507

which was due to the failure of the resistor connected in the electrical circuit. As the 508

current density was derived from recording the potential drop across the resistor, the 509

change in resistance directly affected the calculated current density. Upon replacing a 510

functioning resistor on Day 16, the current density profile went back to normal. During 511

in-series operation, a tiered voltage strategy was applied, with 0.9 V for R1, 0.7 V for 512

R2 and 0.5 V for R3, respectively. The rationale was that since R1 received the highest 513


<!-- Page 29 -->


COD concentration, applying a higher voltage would ensure the optimal H2 production 514

rate. Whereas R2 and R3 were mainly used as a polishing step for the remainder COD 515

that R1 could not degrade. The tiered voltage strategy indeed resulted in a tiered current 516

density profile (Fig. 6B), where R1 reached a maximum current density of 12.5 A m-2, 517

whereas R2 and R3 current density dropped. 518

The COD concentration was measured at the outlet of each module, and COD 519

removal for each module is calculated based on the inlet and outlet COD concentrations. 520

When using synthetic wastewater, the maximum COD removal was 78.4% (Fig. 6C). 521

After switching to PHW-SDW as substrate, the COD removal decreased with the 522

maximum removal being 66.3 ± 10.6% (Fig. 6D). The in-series operation, however, 523

did show higher COD removal under the same HRT. The final effluent (outlet of R3) 524

showed a maximum COD removal of 86.4%. The improvement in COD removal is 525

likely due to better mass transfer and longer retention time, as the flow rate in in-series 526

operation is three times as fast as in-parallel operation to keep the overall HRT the same. 527

The H2 production rate follows the same pattern as current density, as the 𝑟𝑟𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 528

was almost always > 90% throughout the onsite integration. The maximum H2 529

production rate when using synthetic wastewater was 1.1 L Lcat day-1 and increased 530

when substrate was switched to PHW-SDW (Fig. 6E-F). The increased H2 production 531

rate reflected the increased combined current of all three modules, which is likely a 532

result of the higher conductivity of the PHW-SDW compared to synthetic wastewater. 533

During in-parallel operation, the maximum H2 production rate was 1.2 L Lcat day-1. The 534


<!-- Page 30 -->


in-series operation led to tiered H2 production rate, with the highest production rate of 535

the three modules being 1.8, 0.7 and 0.7 L Lcat day-1, respectively. When normalized to 536

the reactor volume, the highest H2 production rate was 0.5 L LR day-1. To the best of 537

our knowledge, this is the highest H2 production rate achieved in pilot MECs with a 538

module volume > 10 L (Fig. S6) (Jiang et al., 2023a). In contrary to COD removal rate, 539

which does not show a clear trend with respect to reactor volume, H2 production rate 540

often drastically scale down as the reactor module increases (Jiang et al., 2023a). 541

However, it should be noted that these results were achieved with a cathodic pH set at 542

4. Theoretically, each unit decrease in cathodic pH reduces the energy requirement of 543

the MEC by 59 mV (Rousseau et al., 2020a; Ruiz et al., 2015). Therefore, a pH of 4 544

would lower the energy requirement by 0.18 V compared to neutral cathodic pH. Some 545

previous works that did not employ pH control could have cathodic pH that rose to> 546

12, leading to significant energy loss. Although pH control would inevitably add to the 547

operational cost, we believe this should be feasible as pH control in electrochemical 548

settings is well-established at industrial scale such as alkaline water electrolysis (Brauns 549

and Turek, 2020). The elevated temperature being used also partly contributed to the 550

good performance. Therefore, it is important to factor in these differences in comparing 551

performance at similar applied voltage. The use of PBS warrants further investigation 552

on the lifecycle environmental benefits, but could be minimized through selection of 553

PHW with suitable strength, and through configuration optimization. 554

# ChatGPT and Environmental Research

**Authors:** Jun-Jie Zhu; Jinyue Jiang; Meiqi Yang; Zhiyong Jason Ren

**Affiliations:** †Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States | ‡Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## ChatGPT: A Conversational AI That Will Fundamentally Change the Way We Find Information

ChatGPT, the latest text-based artificial intelligence (AI) tool, has quickly gained popularity and is poised to revolutionize various aspects of our lives, including education and research. With its advanced natural language processing (NLP) capabilities, ChatGPT can understand and interpret human language like never before, allowing users to ask questions and receive answers in a conversational and intuitive manner. In this Viewpoint, we aim to draw from our NLP research background and share our experience and thoughts about ChatGPT by providing 10 real-world examples from different areas of environmental research. Our objective is to demonstrate how this emerging tool can be leveraged for research purposes while also highlighting potential pitfalls and challenges. By sharing these experiences, we hope to encourage the responsible and effective use of ChatGPT in research and beyond.

The generative pretrained transformer (GPT) is a cutting-edge natural language generation (NLG) model, and its latest iteration, GPT-3.5 (GPT-41 was released on March 14, 2023), was on a massive corpus of textual data, such as books, articles, and Web sites, with billions of model parameters (GPT-3 for the details).2 ChatGPT is a fine-tuned application based on the GPT-3.5 engine at its initial release that uses supervised fine-tuning modeling (learning based on labeled prompt data), reward model construction (ranking the model responses), and proximal policy optimization (a class of reinforcement learning to optimize the reward policy). Two techniques used in ChatGPT are in-context learning and prompt engineering. In-context learning enables the agent to learn and adapt in real time, making it more versatile and capable of handling a wider range of situations. While ChatGPT can respond to a question with no additional hints (zero-shot prompts), its response quality improves by providing additional examples before asking questions (few-shot prompts). Prompt engineering involves designing model inputs, such as questions and statements, to obtain better outputs (i.e., responses).

The popularity of ChatGPT stems from its rapid, informative, and seemingly “intelligent” responses to any questions. However, it is important to question whether the model truly understands the content it produces, because mistakes and errors are also frequently obtained even for simple questions. As a result, it is essential to exercise caution and avoid over- and underestimating the potential and capability of the emerging tool (Figure 1).

*Figure 1: We should leverage the advantages (right side) that ChatGPT offers us while also exercising caution regarding potential hidden pitfalls (left side).*

## What We Found Beneficial and Where We See Potential

### Writing Improvement, Key Points, and Theme Identification

Writing is an essential part of research, and while ChatGPT should not be relied upon as the original content provider, it does provide great benefits in language polishing and identifying errors. This capability is particularly valuable for non-native speakers of the intended language. Moreover, ChatGPT can be used to translate text with more customized requests, and it can be utilized to summarize critical information from lengthy material. For example, by asking ChatGPT to identify key points, synopses, and main themes of a lengthy text, researchers can save time and gain a good understanding of all of the material to facilitate better comprehension (example S1). Alternatively, ChatGPT can generate suggestive titles from summaries or abstracts based on the main text, which may not meet specific needs but will certainly inspire new ideas. For example, we asked for different styles of titles based on the same abstract for tailored uses. The suggested review article titles proposed by ChatGPT were more formal, while the presentation titles were more vivid (example S2). Another valuable feature is that it can assist in adjusting and reducing writing content to meet word limitation requirements.

### Sequential Information Retrieval

As a large language model (LLM), ChatGPT is good at basic information retrieval and concept explanation. When a concept is well-defined and appears in multiple sources during data collection, ChatGPT has a higher probability of explaining it correctly. This makes it particularly valuable for junior researchers who need help understanding complex concepts, such as terminologies, methods, and policies. It is also helpful for senior researchers who need to quickly familiarize themselves with new research areas from a large amount of information when tackling multidisciplinary problems. To test ChatGPT’s abilities on more comprehensive information retrieval, we verified 10 trending-up environmental research topics, including PFAS, microplastics, life cycle assessment, and circular economy, which we previously identified.3,4 ChatGPT successfully explained all concepts correctly on a general level (example S3). One great feature of LLMs (compared to Google or Baidu) is that they can “memorize” previous conversations (≲3000 words for ChatGPT),5 allowing for a series of customized questions to facilitate targeted information acquisition. For example, we tested sequential questions about direct lithium extraction, starting with a general explanation and progressing to specific materials used for selective lithium adsorption, and found the responses informative (example S4).

### Coding, Debugging, and Syntax Explanation

As environmental research increasingly relies on data science, programming skills have become essential. Unfortunately, many environmental researchers lack the necessary training in programming. Fortunately, ChatGPT can assist by suggesting code snippets tailored to specific needs, identifying syntax errors and offering possible fixes, and explaining complicated or unfamiliar syntax to facilitate the learning process. For instance, if one looks to learn Python coding for predicting daily concentrations of organic carbon aerosols based on concentrations of other aerosol pollutants and meteorological conditions (example S5), ChatGPT can help with customized solutions such as data splitting, cross-validation, hyperparameter optimization, and more. Whenever you come across unfamiliar terms or syntax, ChatGPT makes it easy to obtain additional explanations.

## What We Found Problematic and Where We Should Be Cautious

### Fabricated Information and Lack of Updated, Domain Knowledge

The working mechanisms of a LLM determine that it could generate false or fabricated information. Perhaps one of the most significant concerns is that it provides made-up references or sources of specific text, such as fabricated DOI or URL links. Additionally, ChatGPT’s training data extend to only 2021, and as it generates responses without access to the Internet, its limitations are magnified in areas where data are limited, such as the academic literature. As a result, ChatGPT often fails to provide state-of-the-art information in science and engineering.

We illustrated the aforementioned issues through an example in which we posed a series of questions about PFAS to ChatGPT. While ChatGPT was able to provide useful general information about PFAS, such as their physical and chemical properties (example S3), it incorrectly provided the chemical formula for PFOA when asked about the chemical structure of PFAS (example S6). Furthermore, when asked about whether a microbial electrochemical system (MES) was able to degrade PFAS, ChatGPT asserted that MES had been shown to do so (example S7). However, this information was not available to ChatGPT, as the first publication on MES degrading PFAS was released after ChatGPT’s training data cutoff.6 When asked to provide a source for this information, ChatGPT fabricated a seemingly credible literature reference and a made-up DOI that leads to an entirely unrelated article. The same pattern repeated across several devices and accounts, with ChatGPT providing different literature references, none of which were real. More examples demonstrating ChatGPT’s lack of domain knowledge can be found in example S8. As a result, researchers are advised to exercise caution when relying on information from ChatGPT and to always fact-check responses.

### Lack of Accountability in Decision Making

Environmental research involves a multitude of decision-making processes. Despite the constant updates and improvements made to ChatGPT, it is nearly impossible to completely eliminate false or fake information. Moreover, the decision-making process still heavily relies on human wisdom and judgment, and the involvement of AI remains controversial. In fact, researchers have discovered that ChatGPT generates responses with social bias,7 raising doubts about relying on AI to solve environmental issues. As an added level of complexity, AI cannot be held accountable for their decisions, at least not yet. Therefore, caution must be exercised when inviting AI into decision-making processes, especially for environmental problems that are closely tied to public welfare.

Another area of concern in LLM pertains to the training materials used. Because a significant proportion of the corpus is derived from online platforms, there is a possibility that it could be deliberately manipulated to alter the behavior (e.g., poisoning attack8). Despite the filtering and weighting of the source dataset (e.g., the common crawl dataset in GPT-32), as well as ChatGPT’s preset rules to avoid responding to user-induced conspiracy theories, the extent to which it can filter out harmful information from the corpus employed for training remains unclear.

### Opportunity Cost of Relying on ChatGPT

While ChatGPT brings much convenience and many benefits, the use of this tool may result in over-reliance, and its single output without diverse sources and opinions may hinder creative thinking. Traditional search engines offer a list of relevant information, while ChatGPT provides a single response that lacks diversity. Furthermore, depending too much on ChatGPT may impede one’s learning curve for new knowledge. For example, if a trainee relies on the tool to generate programming code, the person may miss learning opportunities and failed to gain skills of their own. This issue is reflected in many schools’ policies that ban or restrict the use of ChatGPT in learning settings.9,10 To what extent ChatGPT should be involved in various tasks is at one’s own discretion, but we recommend using it as an assistant rather than a substitute.

## Advanced Uses of ChatGPT

### Engineering Prompts to Obtain High-Quality Responses

We can and should improve the quality of responses from ChatGPT by using prompt engineering to design better questions. Typical guides include role-play, text format, style or tone, word limit, and other personalized requirements. In this example, we asked ChatGPT to explain “anaerobic digestion” with different engineered prompts (example S9). We asked ChatGPT to play different roles (e.g., presenter, family member, researcher, and professor) and offer different formats or styles of text (e.g., bullet points, short conversation, seminar speech, and reading material with mark-down style). By varying the prompts, we were able to obtain a range of responses that were tailored to different audiences and purposes. This approach enables the generation of high-quality responses that are both informative and engaging, making it a valuable tool for tasks such as content creation and knowledge sharing.

### Few-Shot to Obtain a Fully Customized Response

It is possible to ask ChatGPT to understand self-contained rules for designing designated responses with required formats. For example, we employed ChatGPT and Midjourney (an AI drawing tool) to design and prepare the drawing shown in Figure S1. We first drafted a descriptive text that introduced the rules and formats used for AI drawing using Midjourney (example S10). We then asked ChatGPT to generate customized designing option suffixes for the AI drawing. The subsequent step involved requesting ChatGPT to produce drawing commands using the option suffixes. Finally, we applied the generated command in Midjourney to create and refine the drawing. The example demonstrates that we can utilize ChatGPT to perform more creative work beyond text and code with precise and actionable rules.

## Outlook

Disruptive technologies generate both opportunities and controversies. There is no doubt that ChatGPT will transform the world and make research and other work more automated or streamlined. We should embrace and take advantage of such changes to advance our missions, but we should also exercise caution to avoid pitfalls and recognize the limitations. It is worth noting that many publishers, including the American Chemical Society, have explicitly stated that AI tools like ChatGPT do not qualify for authorship. Any use of AI tools for text or image generation should be disclosed in the manuscript. As newer LLMs (like GPT-4) are introduced, they will become more reliable and capable of handling more complex tasks, which could alleviate some of the current issues. However, our approach to using ChatGPT and other AI tools should remain consistent. Humans are the primary content creators, and AI tools are our assistants, meant to improve the quality of our lives and the environment in which we live.

A B S T R A C T

Microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) have demonstrated high-rate H2 production while concurrently treating wastewater, but the transition in scale from laboratory research to systems that can be practically applied has encountered challenges. It has been more than a decade since the first pilot-scale MEC was reported, and in recent years, many attempts have been made to overcome the barriers and move the technology to the market. This study provided a detailed analysis of MEC scale-up efforts and summarized the key factors that should be considered to further develop the technology. We compared the major scale-up configurations and systematically evaluated their performance from both technical and economic perspectives. We characterized how system scaleup impacts the key performance metrics such as volumetric current density and H2 production rate, and we proposed methods to evaluate and optimize system design and fabrication. In addition, preliminary technoeconomic analysis indicates that MECs can be profitable in many different market scenarios with or without subsidies. We also provide perspectives on future development needed to transition MEC technology to the marketplace.

## 1. Introduction

The increasing demand for clean energy and water is driving the development of new processes and technologies that provide agile and multifaceted solutions. Microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) are a type of microbial electrochemical system that carry unique functions that accomplish concurrent H2 production and organic waste degradation (Logan et al., 2008; Wang and Ren, 2013). Compared to abiotic elec­ trolysis, MEC technology consumes low to zero energy, and it uses wastewater rather than clean water to produce clean H2 (Jack et al., 2021; Rousseau et al., 2020a). MEC reactors have been tested with a vast range of wastewater streams, including domestic wastewater (Escapa et al., 2012a; Heidrich et al., 2014), animal waste slurry (Cerrillo et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2009), and a variety of industrial streams from food and beverage, oil and gas, biorefineries, and fermentation effluents (Chen et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2014). Results from laboratory to pilot scales have demonstrated the potential for MEC technology to be integrated processes to transform wastewater

treatment into an energy neutral or positive process that yields both economic and environmental benefits (Osset-´Alvarez et al., 2019). A typical MEC reactor involves five major components: (1) an anode, (2) a cathode, (3) an electrolyte, (4) a separator/membrane, and 5) a power source. In an MEC, electroactive microorganisms oxidize sub­ strates from the anolyte and transfer electrons (e−) to the anode as the electron acceptor through direct contact or mediated processes (Logan et al., 2019). The electrons are then used at the cathode to reduce H2O or H+ to H2. The whole-cell reaction for MEC using acetate as substrate can thus be written as:

This difference in EO cell highlights the much lower voltage needed in MEC to drive H2 evolution compared to abiotic water electrolysis. The theoretical energy requirement for MEC is as low as 3.3 kWh⋅kg−1 H2 (0.29 kWh⋅m−3 H2) (Logan et al., 2008), which is more than 90% less than the 39 kWh⋅kg−1 H2 needed for water electrolysis (Ivy, 2004). In addition, because the MEC anode does not produce O2, traditional ion exchange membranes can be omitted to save cost and prevent fouling. Such single-chamber configuration however does generate different sets of challenges such as reduced H2 purity due to CO2 generation from the anode, as well as H2 consumption due to methanogenesis (Call and Logan, 2008; Guo et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009). Many studies have reported on advances in MEC development, but most of the studies are still at the laboratory scale with the volume rarely exceeding 1 L. The first scale-up trial of MEC was published in 2011 with a 1000 L reactor (Cusick et al., 2011), after which dozens of pilot studies demonstrated system performance at different reactor configurations, scales, and operational modes. A recent review benchmarked the per­ formance of pilot scale MECs against standard activated sludge pro­ duced during wastewater treatment reported that MECs can treat actual wastewater to effluent standards at a lower energetic cost, but the volumetric treatment rate and reactor depth are the main limiting fac­ tors that prevent commercial application (Leicester et al., 2020a).

Similarly, multiple reviews have summarized the substrates, materials, and reactor performance of pilot-scale studies (Escapa et al., 2016; Kadier et al., 2016; Rousseau et al., 2020a), but the pathway towards scale-up and cost feasibility remains unclear. Therefore, we focused this analytical review on breaking down the mainstream MEC scale-up strategies employed to date. Our review revealed the major technolog­ ical barriers to large system manufacturing and operation. In addition, we evaluated the profitability of MECs under different cost scenarios using techno-economic analysis (TEA) and discussed perspectives on how to finally push this technology to the marketplace. We focused on the studies with total operational volumes larger than 1 L, and for each entry, we summarized available information regarding reactor design, operation conditions, and performance metrics (See Supplementary Table).

## 2. The pilot MEC design schemes

Many groups have reported their pilot MEC configurations, but they can be divided into two major categories: reactor-based or electrodebased modularization (Fig. 1). The concept of reactor modularization was realized by hydraulically connecting several reactor units in series or in parallel to achieve a higher overall volume. When connected in series, the hydraulic retention time was maximized, which could lead to better organic removal, but the treatment capacity was limited. When connected in parallel, treatment capacity and overall H2 production could be increased, but the wastewater treatment efficiency may be limited. ## 3. The pilot MEC performance metrics

3.1. Would reactor size and modularization approach make a difference?

Pilot MECs have been actively researched and tested, but their per­ formance inevitably varied significantly. To examine if reactor size was a determining factor, we used key performance metrics including COD removal efficiency, current density, and H2 production rate to evaluate

3.2. The current density barrier and how to overcome it in pilot reactors

The volumetric H2 production rate reporting liters of H2 produced per liter of reactor per day (L⋅LR −1⋅day−1) has long been used as an important performance metric since the early days of MECs (Call and Logan, 2008; Cheng and Logan, 2007). The use of volumetric rate fol­ lows the tradition in wastewater treatment as MECs were not only used for H2 production but also as a wastewater treatment technology. Such volumetric-based H2 rate is different from the common electrode surface area-based current density (A⋅m−2 or mA⋅cm−2), as traditional water electrolysis does not consider water treatment as a function. The elec­ trolysis community often views that MECs have limited applications as they operate at very low surface area-based current density. However, one should note the cathode reaction in MECs is the same as abiotic electrolysis as the microbial anode reaction is generally the limiting factor. In large-scale applications, anodes with much larger surface areas per unit of cross-sectional area are feasible and, as such will enable much faster wastewater organic removal as well as higher overall current and resulting higher cathode surface area-based current density. There are a variety of reasons for the discrepancy between laboratory-scale and pilot-scale reactor performance, even if the con­ figurations are similar. Laboratory-scale reactors often have more ideal flow profiles and architecture, whereas larger reactors possess hydraulic dead zones, electrode blockage, and are more prone to leakage. In addition, the internal resistance of large reactors remains high due to the relatively low conductivity of wastewater as well as increased ohmic resistance of large carbon electrodes (Heidrich et al., 2014). Larger electrode spacings and loose connections are more likely to occur in large reactors as well (Guo et al., 2017; Rousseau et al., 2020b). One important factor that has largely been omitted was the heterogeneity induced by large reactors. Hydrostatic pressure, solid deposition, and dissolved O2 concentrations could be exacerbated in large systems, creating vastly different micro-environments throughout the reactor. For example, San-Martín et al. (2019b) reported vertical stratification of anode microbial communities in two 16 L MECs, with distinct variation at the family taxonomic level observed across electrode sampling points. In laboratory-scale reactors, it is generally assumed that electrostatic potential would be homogeneous along the electrode surface as well as in the bulk electrolyte, but those conditions may not hold true for larger-scale systems. Potential differences along the electrode surface can be compensated using metal current collectors, which is currently adopted by many pilot-scale studies (Carmona-Martínez et al., 2015;

As a result, such a heterogeneous electrode potential could lead to unfavorable growth of non-electroactive microorganisms and high electrical potential loss (Torres et al., 2009).

5.2. Sufficient and standard data collection and reporting are needed

Although there are well-established guidelines for reporting MEC results in laboratory-scale studies (Logan et al., 2008), results from pilot studies often vary widely. It is certainly difficult to perform compre­ hensive measurements on all key parameters in large systems, but to advance the technology, coordinated and standard reporting of key parameters would be very valuable. Fig. 8B summarizes 10 common MEC metrics and the number of pilot MEC studies that reported these metrics. The reactor assembly including size, material, and configura­ tion is almost always reported. Current density is also reported for almost all existing pilot literature studies, either normalized by volume or surface area. However, the reporting method is not consistent, as some studies chose to report absolute current expressed in amps or milliamps without normalization, which prohibits a fair comparison across studies (Jadhav et al., 2022a). Though current density can be calculated if volume or surface information were given, unfortunately they are not all provided in the cited studies. Also, some studies only report current or current density but do not report on H2 production data, which is certainly highly desirable. As noted previously, high current density did not necessarily lead to high levels of H2 recovery due to leaking, re-consumption, and other practical challenges. Efficiency metrics, including rcat and coulombic efficiency (CE), are reported in even lower frequency. These two metrics can be useful in­ dicators of MEC system malfunctions as well as side reactions. A CE greater than 100% indicates that an alternate electron donor is present and is contributing to the current. In most cases, a CE >100% indicates H2 recycling; that is, H2 can be directly oxidized either in the anode or is consumed by homoacetogens and converted to acetate or

Under such scenarios, the findings suggest that current pilot MECs are not profitable unless working with a very high EPR, but the reduced cost associated with wastewater treatment will give MECs a major advantage over other electrolysis approaches. ## 5. What it takes to make MECs market-relevant

5.1. High-strength wastewater would be an ideal entry point

Most pilot MECs used actual wastewater as electrolyte, but as mentioned, the ionic conductivity has been a major hurdle in large-scale reactors. Fig. 8A summarizes the relationship between wastewater ionic conductivity and current density reported by pilot-scale MECs, and it clearly depicts that higher conductivity led to higher current density. Higher conductivity reduces the system internal resistance and facilitates ion transfer, and that is why almost all synthetic electrolytes used buffer solutions (Kadier et al., 2016; Sleutels et al., 2009). Some studies added salts to improve wastewater MEC conductivity, but caution should be taken as non-buffering salts such as NaCl will compete with buffering components in the ion-migration flux and exacerbate local acidification at the bioanode, which causes unfavorable thermodynamics and irreversibly deteriorating bioanode activity (Oliot et al., 2016; Satinover et al., 2020; Torres et al., 2008). Adding buffering salt can alleviate such problems, but the cost can be prohibitive. The highest current densities achieved in pilot-scale MECs so far, including 90 A⋅m− 2

reported by Rousseau et al. (2020b) and 42.3 A⋅m− 2 by Carmona-- Martínez et al. (2015), were both obtained with a high salt electrolyte (i. e., 45 g⋅L− 1 and 35 g⋅L− 1 NaCl addition, respectively) and halotolerant

using actual wastewater is another major challenge to overcome for realworld applications. It has been documented before that long-term operation could lead to performance drop for a variety of reasons (Heidrich et al., 2014). One of the top reasons is the competition from methanogenesis, as methanogens in the electrolyte will grow and oxidize acetate, formate, or H2 as the electron donor for the production of methane. A recent review provided a great summary of the strategies to inhibit methanogenesis, including shortening hydraulic retention time, harvesting H2 out, lowering the temperature, and controlling pH (He et al., 2022). Another cause of reduced performance is the defi­ ciency in micronutrients like minerals that are required for sustaining microbial activity, which can be resolved by periodical supplementa­ tion, though the cost needs to be carefully considered. Other reasons may include influent toxicity, electrode potential deviation, and biofilm deterioration. The constant monitoring of the electrode potential, elec­ troactive biofilm, temperature and pH, and other parameters would be critical to detect and address these problems. For example, monitoring the anode potential could help in deciding the appropriate applied voltage, as a proper range of anode potential is vital to biofilm perfor­ mance. In large-scale operations, it is not uncommon to switch between different modes of power supply. During the inoculation stage, a lower set anode potential helps accelerate electroactive biofilm formation. After that, a higher potential could reduce energy input, facilitate organic degradation, and increase overall current and H2 production (Ren et al., 2011). Beside electrochemical measures, biofilm monitoring using imaging or omics tools could also provide valuable information on the viability and composition of the biofilm and shed light on the longevity of reactor operation. From such a perspective, the reactor design should consider the easy accessibility of the individual electrodes for sampling and monitoring without operation interruption. Beside these direct measurements, a periodic check on rcat and CE is also rec­ ommended as discussed in Section 5.2.

## 6. To H2 and beyond

More than 10 years have passed since the first scale-up of MEC technology. Since then, we have seen increasing interest in bringing MEC closer to industrial application. We have witnessed great progress along the way, although some challenges remain unsolved for pilot studies. The current density needs to be further increased; however, this is limited by the metabolic rate of the microbes. The incorporation of thermophilic strains while increasing the reactor temperature might provide an interesting solution. Thermophiles usually have a higher metabolic rate compared to strains that thrive at room temperature and thus can sustain a higher current density in the microbial electro­ chemical system. Moreover, the incorporation of thermophiles can take advantage of some high-temperature industrial waste streams while probably avoiding methanogens at the same time. It has also been proposed that thermophiles might be able to degrade a broader spec­ trum of organic compounds, including some recalcitrant species that are resistant to microbial degradation at room temperature (Rathinam et al., 2019). Beside thermophilic strains, halophilic bacteria could also play an important role. In Section 5.1, we discussed the importance of con­ ductivity in improving current. Therefore, the use of high-strength wastewaters as electrolytes, along with halophilic bacteria, is worth considering. We have seen an increasing number of studies in which a halophilic biofilm was inoculated from saline environments (Carmo­ na-Martínez et al., 2015; Rousseau et al., 2020b). On the other hand, thermophilic studies remain scarce. Selection by creating a niche that is favorable to the strains wanted has been the primary way for inoculating a bioanode with specific traits so far. Genetic engineering might aid in this process to create microbes that meet the aforementioned criteria. Beside high temperatures, operating MECs under elevated pressure is another strategy worth considering. A low rcat could indicate H2 leakage, as it is often harder to sustain a gas-tight reactor condition on a larger scale. In a few rare cases, a rcat values >100% has been observed. These examples clearly support that such efficiency metrics are necessary parameters to be measured and reported. The least reported metrics among the list are energy-related parameters. As discussed in the TEA, assessing energy consumption or energy efficiency is important in determining the economic feasibility of the technology, and many times, this is a major advantage of MECs compared to abiotic water electrolysis. The energy consumption metrics can be calculated from the voltage applied and the current generated, and they should be reported and highlighted more. Overall, we can minimize bias by forming a more comprehensive and standardized reporting convention; therefore, we prepared Table S2 that lists all the variables and metrics that we believe should be reported in pilot-scale MEC studies and explains how they can be obtained. For research articles that focus on technical advancement, metrics in Table S2 can be prioritized in reporting, and for those discussing economics of the technology and comparing against competing technologies, Table S1 could be used.

5.3. Balance the pros and cons of scale-up configurations

While each MEC reactor scale-up approach has its advantages and challenges, the quantitative analyses provided in this study shed some light on key considerations. Fig. 8C summarizes the strengths and weaknesses of each configuration discussed, and several major considerations are worthy of discussion. First, modularized cathode assembly appears to be effective in obtaining high current levels and preventing H2 leakage and re-consumption, so if its cost can be reduced, such a design can be promising. On the other hand, single-chamber systems would encounter difficulties in actual open wastewater conditions due to methanogenesis and contamination unless those barriers could be overcome. Second, the flow pattern may be an easy parameter to optimize, as hydrodynamic analysis can help improve kinetics, reduce dead zones, and improve conversion efficiency. Such analysis has been carried out in laboratory-scale reactors (Gao et al., 2021, 2020; Hern´andez-García et al., 2020), and can be applied in pilot-scale reactors. Many pilot-scale MEC studies use electrode modules and placed them on alternate sides of the reactor body to act as baffles, thus forming a serpentine flow pattern. This design resembles the disinfection contact tanks and prolongs contact time to improve COD conversion via a plug-flow configuration. The electrode assemblies at the front of the reactor will encounter heavy organic loadings and will generate most of the H2, while modules at the back end of the reactor may suffer from insufficient electron donors. Other considerations worth noting include the difficulty in bioanode inoculation for large reactors. Several studies have mentioned that the inoculation stage took much longer than laboratory-scale reactors, from weeks to several months (Brown et al., 2014; Cusick et al., 2011; Escapa et al., 2015; San-Martín et al., 2019b). Modularizing the electrodes, therefore, would provide a unique advantage in introducing faster inoculation, as the individual electrode modules can be inoculated separately in smaller containers first before transferring them into the large reactors. However, to the best of our knowledge, such a practice has not been tested in pilot-scale studies.

The distinct advantage of producing clean H2 at a low energy requirement while cleaning wastewater provides an exciting future for incorporating MEC technology into the (waste)water industry. In fact, MEC’s prede­ cessor—microbial fuel cell—has already been commercialized for a few years. Aquacycl LLC has employed reactor modules to expand their microbial fuel cells to a treatment capacity of 570 L of swine wastewater per day (Babanova et al., 2021). Similarly, some other variations of microbial electrochemical systems have also been commercialized in recent years, as summarized by Jadhav et al. (2022b). As the perfor­ mance of pilot-scale MECs continues to improve, the widespread commercialization and deployment of MEC systems for wastewater treatment and H2 generation should not come as a surprise in the near future.

Operating at an elevated pressure can yield pressurized H2 directly from MEC, which saves the energy needed for downstream compression, and the H2 produced can be readily available for use or sale. Most currently available commercial proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers already operate with an outlet pressure of 30–40 bars (Hancke et al., 2022). Operating a MEC process under such pressure would make it more competitive compared to existing technology. However, high-pressure conditions could also give rise to safety concerns and potential leakages, for which experience from the water electrolysis industry could potentially offer valuable insights. Beside experimental research, modeling is also crucial to advancing our understanding of MECs. Past models have provided valuable information regarding the mass transfer (Yan et al., 2021), potential distribution (Lacroix et al., 2014), biofilm kinetics (Kato Marcus et al., 2007; Pinto et al., 2011; Rimboud et al., 2015), and electrode topography (Champigneux et al., 2018). However, there are some aspects that are less modeled but could shed light on future pilot design. For example, hydraulic modeling of pilot-scale MECs can provide guidance on eliminating hydraulic dead zones and improving mass transfer. In recent years, machine learning has evolved as a powerful tool for environmental researchers (Hino et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2021). We have started to see its application in the MET field as well (Cai et al., 2019; Du et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2013; Lesnik and Liu, 2017). We believe that machine learning could provide exciting insights into pilot-scale MEC designs in the future; however, incorporating machine learning should be done with caution. Most notably, datasets should be sufficient in size to enable the development of a meaningful machine learning model. Other problems such as data leakage and confounding variables should be handled carefully to avoid misleading results (Riley, 2019; Whalen et al., 2022). While the bulk of pilot MEC studies is dedicated to wastewater treatment and H2 recovery, several pilot-scale MECs are built for other functions. For instance, Sim et al. Hydrothermal liquefaction presents a promising approach for the conversion of wet waste into biocrude and biofuels. However, the post-hydrothermal liquefaction wastewater poses signiﬁcant challenges for

treatment and valorization due to its high concentration and complex nature. In this study, we investigated

the conversion pathways of major organic contaminants within the microbial electrolytic treatment of wastewater from food waste hydrothermal liquefaction. To achieve this, we employed high-performance

liquid chromatography and 2D nuclear magnetic resonance. Our ﬁndings demonstrate volatile fatty acids

and monohydric and polyhydric alcohols were eﬀectively transformed through the synergistic metabolism of fermentative and electroactive bacteria, which led to over 70% chemical oxygen demand removal of

the recalcitrant compounds and a record high H2 production rate (1.62 L L−1 d−1). We also employed the

liquid-state 15N nuclear magnetic resonance on wastewater samples for the ﬁrst time and revealed that the nitrogen-containing heteroaromatics were persistent to microbial electrochemical treatment. By inte-

that provides insights for enhancing treatment eﬃciency and facilitating resource recovery.

## 1. Introduction

The urgent needs for carbon circularity highlight the necessity for clean energy alternatives beyond conventional fossil fuels. Among these alternatives, hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) emerged as a promising technology for converting wet waste, such as food waste, algal biomass, and animal manure into biocrude, which can be further refined into jet fuel through hydrotreatment using H2 as a reducing agent.1 However, the HTL process generates a highly concentrated stream, known as post-hydrothermal liquefaction wastewater (PHW), which has high organic concentrations and high N content. According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), the valorization of PHW is one of the key improvements that need to be made to achieve the targeted fuel selling price of $3 per gallon gasoline equivalent performance goal.2 Previous study identified a wide

array of organic molecules including carboxylic acids, alcohols, ketones, aldehydes, phenolics, esters, ethers, amides and heterocyclic compounds as the primary constituents of PHW.3

The complex organic matrix, particularly the nitrogenous organic compounds, pose challenges to traditional wastewater treatment and exhibit potential cytotoxicity.4

Previous studies have explored various approaches for PHW treatment, and extraction of value-added chemicals was reported from PHW derived from simple substrates such as rice straw5,6 or with model PHW solution.7 However, the complexity of PHW presents barriers in terms of increased separation cost and diﬃculty. Gasification, for example, can reduce organics while producing H2 and CH4,8–10 but the energy needs for drying and operation can be prohibitive. Anaerobic fermentation, on the other hand, converts organics to CH4- rich biogas, but the performance was inhibited due to PHW toxicity.11,12 Microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) has been recently investigated in treating recalcitrant wastewater and recovering high rate H2,13–16 and it demonstrated a good synergy with HTL, because not only the aqueous phase can be cleaned via microbial electrochemical process, the produced high quality H2 can be used onsite for biocrude upgrading. ## 2. Experimental section

2.1. HTL PHW feedstock

The HTL system used in generating the PHW is located at the Process Development Laboratory in the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL). Food waste slurry Engineered Bioslurry (EBS®) was obtained from Waste Management Inc. as the HTL feedstock. The slurry was pretreated with JWC muﬃn monster and Hockmeyer immersion mill to improve homogeneity and pumpability. The modular HTL system is divided into areas for feedstock preparation and staging, hydrothermal liquefaction, and product separation. The feed rate was set at 12 L h−1 with a liquid hourly space velocity of 4 L L−1 h−1. The HTL was performed at a temperature of 349 °C and a pressure of 192 bar (2790 psig), with a time on stream of 24 h. The generated PHW was collected and stored in −20 °C before shipping for MEC studies.

2.2. MEC construction and operation

Two-chamber MECs were used for all the PHW experiments. The cell modules are acrylic cubes with cylindrical inner chamber of 5 cm diameter. Carbon brush anodes (5 cm in diameter, 5 cm in length) and platinized titanium sheet cathodes (Fuel Cell Store, USA) with a dimension of 3 × 4 cm were used in all tests. The anode and cathode chambers have a working volume of 90 mL and 30 mL respectively, and are separated with a bipolar membrane (Fumasep FBM, FumaTech, Germany) to balance out pH gradient. ## 3. Results and discussion

3.1. PHW characterization and treatment by MEC

The detailed characteristics of the PHW generated from HTL processing food waste are shown in Table S1.† The wastewater contained highly concentrated organics, and the COD value was 57 500 ± 200 mg L−1, approximately two orders of magnitude higher than domestic wastewater. The DOC content of the PHW was 17 853 ± 287 mg L−1. The COD and DOC value combined will give an average degree of reduction of carbon of 4.8, marking the average carbon in PHW is slightly more reduced than biomass. The water was slightly alkalic with a pH of 7.97, and the conductivity was 18.4 mS cm−1, indicating high ionic strength. Both inorganic salts and ionizable organic compounds such as VFAs contribute to the conductivity. The total inorganic concentration of the PHW was 404 ± 12 mg L−1, which includes carbonate (CO3 2−), bicarbonate (HCO3 −) and dissolved CO2. The high conductivity and high alkalinity are beneficial to MEC treatment, as they facilitate electron transfer and provide high buﬀering capacity to alleviate pH gradient between electrode chambers.22,23

A tailored HPLC database was built to characterize the organic compounds in the PHW (Table S2†), and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and alcohols were identified as the primary organic groups. Acetate (4319 ± 6 mg L−1) and glycerol (4992 ± 253 mg L−1) were the species that had the highest concentrations. VFAs such as acetate were generated during HTL via several diﬀerent routes, including hydrolysis of lipid and deamination of amino acids.1 Acetate could also originate from the acetyl group of the hemicellulose backbone.24 Glycerol, on the other hand, almost exclusively came from the hydrolysis of lipids. The high concentration of glycerol also indicates a high proportion of lipids in the original food waste feedstock. Besides acetate, other VFAs such as propionate, butyrate and isovalerate are also present in significant amounts. Longerchain VFAs, on the other hand, tend to partition into the bio-

2.3. Chemical characterization

The raw PHW and treated eﬄuent from MEC were analyzed by a HPLC (Agilent 1260 Infinity II, Agilent Technologies, USA) with an ion-exclusion column (Hi-Plex H, Agilent Technologies, USA) and a refractive index detector. 4 mM H2SO4 solution was used as mobile phase running at a flow rate of 0.6 mL min−1. External standards were used to establish elution time as well as standard curves for calculating concentrations from signal area. COD, total nitrogen (TN), ammonia-nitrogen (NH3-N) and nitrate-nitrogen (NO3-N) were measured using standard Hach TNT and TNTplus protocol (Hach Company, USA). Organic nitrogen (ORG-N) concentrations were calculated by subtracting NH3-N and NO3-N concentrations from TN concentrations. Nitrite-nitrogen concentrations were always below detection limit for all samples. The dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and inorganic carbon (IC) concentrations were determined by a TOC analyzer (Shimadzu, Japan). The heterocyclic compounds were analyzed using Agilent 5975C GC-MS with Agilent HP-5MS 30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm film thickness with helium as carrier gas at 1.0 mL min−1. Oven temperature was initially held for 0.1 min at 35 °C, ramped at 6 °C min−1 with a final temperature of 325 °C. Final oven hold of 1 minute was used. The inlet was heated at 270 °C and 1 μL of sample was injected using a splitless injection. To prepare the samples for NMR characterization, we first filtered PHW through 0.22 μm filter, then pipette 5 mL of filtrate to a tube. We then froze-dry the samples overnight and redissolve the sample with D2O (3 mL unless otherwise noted). The sample was then transferred to an NMR tube. 1H, 1H–13C HSQC NMR experiments were conducted using a 500 MHz instrument equipped with cryoprobe (Bruker, USA). The number of scans were 16 times with 1024 points in the 1H dimension and 512 points in the 13C dimension. The pulse delay time was 1.3 s. For 1H–15N heteronuclear multiple bond correlation (HMBC) experiments, a 10 times higher concentration factor is used by increasing the amount of filtrate while using the same amount of D2O. The number of scans were 16 times with 2048 points in the 1H dimension and 512 points in the 15N dimension for HMBC experiments. The pulse delay was 1.7 s. The acquired spectra were then processed with Mnova software following standard processing steps including apodization, zero filling and phase correction.

3.3. 2D NMR, SEC, and GC-MS reveals detailed molecular transformation

While COD provided general measures of organic removal and HPLC provided concentration changes on selected compounds based on an existing library, they both have limitations on understanding the broader picture of organic transformation present in the complex PHW.40 Therefore, we employed NMR spectroscopy to reveal a more complete spectrum of the conversion process. Rather than adopting the common 1H NMR that has been used in wastewater characterization, we applied 1H–13C HSQC NMR that probes the proton-carbon single bond correlations on the raw PHW and the eﬄuent after MEC treatment. This is because the narrow chemical shift range (commonly from 0–12 ppm) in 1H NMR may result in signal overlap in complex organic samples such as PHW.41 As shown in Fig. 3A, the raw PHW exhibited a high structural diversity with 1H signal spanning from 0.5–8.5 ppm and 13C signal spanning from 0–150 ppm. The most prominent peaks came from the region which indicates HnCO structures (δH/δC 3.0–4.5/ 50–90 ppm) including monohydric/polyhydric alcohols and ethers. Among them, three peaks which correspond to glycerol are clearly visible with blue ones indicating the terminal CH2 group and the red one indicating the middle CH group. The compounds which were identified by HPLC analysis were mapped towards the HSQC spectrum. Unsurprisingly, the compounds identified by HPLC only constitute a small portion of the visible peaks, further confirming the necessity of NMR on capturing comprehensive chemical information in wastewater. Most notably, many peaks residing in the region indicating HnCO structures were not mapped to HPLC-quantified chemicals. This suggests that besides those in the tailored HPLC database, other alcohols or ethers may also be present in the PHW. Besides HnCO structures, a significant number of peaks were present in the aromatic region (δH/δC 6.5–8.0/ 100–150 ppm) which were not detected by HPLC, indicating a high concentration of aromatic compounds. Overall, the HSQC spectrum provides an intuitive visualization of the chemical information contained in the PHW, and this advantage is even more significant when the spectra across time were combined and animated. 3.4. Biofilm ecology and metabolic network

A compact layer of biofilm was observed on the anode carbon fibers after MEC operation (Fig. 4A).
